info.name: agency-api
info.description:
Hono API on Cloudflare Workers. Every /v1 endpoint requires an API key: Authorization: Bearer ak_pub_... (set the `apiKey` variable once — collection or environment — all requests inherit it).

Public endpoints work with any valid key; what a key can do comes from its user's config (bucketName/publicBaseUrl for uploads, emailDomain for emails, allowedOrigins for where its keys may be called from). /v1/admin/* requires a key whose user has type "admin".

## Key types

A key's type is encoded in its prefix, and decides whether the origin check applies:

- `ak_pub_` — **public key.** Safe to embed in a client website: it only works when the request carries an Origin matching that user's allowedOrigins (bare domain "acme.com" or exact origin "https://acme.com"). Anything else gets 403 ACCESS_DENIED. A public key with an empty allowedOrigins is denied everywhere.
- `ak_ser_` — **server key.** No origin check at all: accepted from any origin, or from a server-side caller that sends no Origin. Never ship one to a browser — anyone who reads it can use it from anywhere. Use it for backend-to-backend calls, cron jobs, and scripts.

Keys issued before this split start with `ak_live_`. They still authenticate and behave exactly like `ak_pub_` keys.

Admin users' keys skip the origin check regardless of type (that's why Postman works). All keys, both types, are rate-limited to 60 req/min each.

Every sent email is logged to the user's history (GET /v1/emails) with the rendered HTML archived in private storage, readable via a 15-min presigned link (GET /v1/emails/:id/html).

Switch between localhost and production with the environment dropdown (local / production). With No Environment selected, requests hit production (collection-variable default).

## Errors

Every error uses one standard shape:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "USER_NOT_FOUND", "message": "No user with email \"x@y.com\"", "cause": "how to fix it (optional)" } }
```

`code` is stable and machine-readable (UPPER_SNAKE_CASE) — branch on it, not on `message`. Common codes: MISSING_API_KEY, UNKNOWN_API_KEY, API_KEY_REVOKED (401) · ACCESS_DENIED (403, origin not allowed — deliberately vague message; only ever returned for public keys), ADMIN_REQUIRED, BUCKET_NOT_CONFIGURED, EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_CONFIGURED, SENDER_DOMAIN_MISMATCH (403) · VALIDATION_FAILED, INVALID_JSON, MISSING_EMAIL_PARAM, MISSING_USERID_PARAM, INVALID_PATH, INVALID_KEY, INVALID_CURSOR (400) · USER_NOT_FOUND, API_KEY_NOT_FOUND, EMAIL_NOT_FOUND, ROUTE_NOT_FOUND (404) · DUPLICATE_EMAIL (409) · RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (429) · EMAIL_PROVIDER_ERROR, STORAGE_DELETE_FAILED, STORAGE_LIST_FAILED (502) · INTERNAL_ERROR, STORAGE_NOT_CONFIGURED, EMAIL_NOT_CONFIGURED (500).

request.description:
Public, no auth. Returns the latest health-cron result from KV (the cron deep-checks DB/KV/SES/R2 every 10 minutes).

status values:
- healthy — last cron run passed all checks (200)
- degraded — last cron run had failing checks; see lastCheck.checks for which and why (503)
- stale — no cron write for >25 min, the cron itself isn't running (503)
- unknown — no cron result yet, e.g. right after deploy (200)

For a live on-demand probe use GET /v1/admin/health instead.

"Which key am I holding?" Returns the calling key's prefix, its derived type, and the full user record (type, bucketName, publicBaseUrl, emailDomain, allowedOrigins).

```json
{ "keyPrefix": "ak_pub_a1b2c3", "keyType": "public", "user": { … } }
```

`keyType` is `"public"` for `ak_pub_` keys (and legacy `ak_live_` ones) or `"server"` for `ak_ser_` keys. Useful for confirming a client is actually using the kind of key you think it is — a `"server"` here on a key that lives in browser JavaScript means it's exposed and should be rotated.

Uploads go to YOUR user's bucket — no bucket field. Max 50 MB. contentLength must be the file's exact byte size (signed into the URL).

**naming** — how the object key is built:
- `filename` (default) → `avatars/photo.jpg`
- `uuid` → `avatars/<uuid>.jpg`
- `uuid-filename` → `avatars/<uuid>-photo.jpg`

In `filename` mode an existing object with the same name returns **409 `FILE_ALREADY_EXISTS`** — pass `"overwrite": true` to replace it. UUID modes never collide.

Response includes uploadUrl (PUT the file there with the returned headers, no auth header) and publicUrl (store this — uploadUrl expires in 15 min). For hands-on testing use the repo's index.html upload tester.

`key` accepts **either** form:

- bare object key: `"avatars/photo.jpg"`
- any full URL of the file: your publicBaseUrl, a `pub-….r2.dev` URL, an R2 endpoint / presigned URL — the URL's path becomes the key (query string ignored). The host is not checked; deletes only ever target your own bucket.

Responses:
- **204** — deleted. Idempotent: also 204 when the key didn't exist (no existence check on purpose).
- **400 `INVALID_KEY`** — URL contains no object path

request.description: Lists your bucket's objects. Each object's `url` is its **durable public URL** (your publicBaseUrl + key) — no expiration, safe to store and share. `prefix` filters by folder; `cursor` paginates via the previous response's `nextCursor`.

from must be @ your user's emailDomain (admins exempt). to accepts a string or an array. Returns 202 { id } (SES MessageId).

Every send is logged to your email history (List emails) with an HTML copy archived in private storage — fetch it via Get email HTML link.

Contact-form submission for public sites. The server renders the notification email (name, message, source, device, IP, reply button) and delivers it to **your account email** — the caller never chooses the recipient, so a browser-exposed key can't spam anyone. The visitor's `email` becomes the Reply-To.

- `subject` optional — defaults to `New contact from {name}`.
- `source` optional — defaults to the request `Origin` header, then "Contact Form".
- `metadata` optional — any extra form fields your site collects (string/number/boolean values, max 25 keys, strings ≤ 2000 chars). Rendered as a "Details" section in the email exactly as sent.
- Device/IP are read from `User-Agent` / `CF-Connecting-IP`.
- Requires your user to have `emailDomain` configured (sender is `noreply@<emailDomain>`), else 403 `EMAIL_DOMAIN_NOT_CONFIGURED`.

**Rate limit: 5 requests per 10 minutes per IP** (Workers KV backed; runs before auth; skipped on localhost so local testing is never throttled). Exceeding it returns 429 `RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`. On top of that, every key allows 60 requests/min.

Every contact email lands in your email history (List emails, `kind: "contact"` with `visitorEmail`/`source`) with the rendered HTML archived — view it via Get email HTML link.

query.description: ISO timestamp cursor — pass the createdAt of the last row to page back

request.description:
Your own email history, newest first — every email the API sent for your user (both Send email and Send contact email).

Each row: `{ id, kind ("send" | "contact"), from, to, subject, messageId, visitorEmail?, source?, createdAt }`. `visitorEmail`/`source` are set on contact-form emails only.

Pagination: response is `{ "emails": [...] }`; to page back, resend with `before=<createdAt of the last row>`.

The rendered HTML of each email is archived — get a link via **Get email HTML link** with the row's `id`.

Returns a presigned URL for one archived email's HTML: `{ "url": "…", "expiresIn": 900 }`. Open the URL in a browser to see the email exactly as sent. The link dies after 15 minutes — request a fresh one anytime.

`:id` is the row id from List emails. 404 `EMAIL_NOT_FOUND` when the id doesn't exist or isn't yours (admins can fetch any).

The archive bucket is private — this endpoint is the only way to read it.

item.name: Admin

request.description:
Fill in and send — every field ready:

- **email** (required) — unique, identifies the user
- **name** — display name
- **type** — "user" | "admin" (admins bypass the email-domain check, can call /v1/admin/*, and their keys skip the origin check)
- **keyType** — type of the key minted below: "public" (default, `ak_pub_…`) or "server" (`ak_ser_…`). Public is origin-secured and meant for the client's website; server skips the origin check entirely and must stay server-side. Omitting this always gives a public key.
- **bucketName** + **publicBaseUrl** — set BOTH or remove both. R2 bucket uploads go to + public URL objects are served from. No bucket needed? Delete both lines.
- **emailDomain** — domain the user may send email as (from: *@domain). Delete the line to disable sending.
- **allowedOrigins** — origin rules this user's **public** keys may be called from (admins and `ak_ser_` keys exempt). Each entry is either a bare domain — `"acme.com"` matches any scheme, port, and subdomain (https://acme.com, https://www.acme.com, …) — or an exact origin like `"https://acme.com"` / `"http://localhost:5173"` (lowercase, no path or trailing slash, no `*`; max 20). Defaults to `[]`, which means the user's public keys are dead until origins are set. Wrong/missing origin → 403 `ACCESS_DENIED`.

Response (201) = full user row **plus a freshly minted API key**:

```json
{ "id": "…", "email": "…", …, "apiKey": { "id": "…", "prefix": "ak_pub_a1b2c3", "key": "ak_pub_…", "type": "public" } }
```

Copy `apiKey.key` and hand it to the client — no separate Create key call needed. Recoverable later via Lookup user by email. Need both a browser key and a server key? Create the user, then use Create key for the second one.

Any subset of the create fields. Set bucketName + publicBaseUrl together; send null for both to remove bucket access.

There is no `keyType` here — a key's type is fixed when it's minted. To switch a client between a public and a server key, create the new key (Keys > Create key) and revoke the old one.

**allowedOrigins** replaces the whole array (not a merge) — send the full list each time; send `[]` to kill all the user's **public** keys. `ak_ser_` server keys and admin users' keys ignore allowedOrigins entirely, so emptying the list does not disable them. Each entry is either:

- a bare domain — `"acme.com"` matches any scheme, port, and subdomain (https://acme.com, http://acme.com, https://www.acme.com, …)
- an exact origin — `"https://acme.com"` or `"http://localhost:5173"` (lowercase, no path or trailing slash, no `*`)

```json
{ "allowedOrigins": ["acme.com", "http://localhost:5173"] }
```
Hard delete. The user's API keys are deleted too (cascade).

request.description:
One-stop handoff lookup: returns the full user row plus a `keys` array with every ACTIVE key decrypted ({ id, prefix, type, key, lastUsedAt, createdAt }). Revoked keys are excluded. Empty `keys` array means the user has no active key — create one via Keys > Create key.

`type` is `"public"` (`ak_pub_`, or a legacy `ak_live_` key) or `"server"` (`ak_ser_`). Check it before handing a key over: a public key only works from the user's allowedOrigins, a server key works from anywhere and must not go into a browser.

The Visualize tab renders this as a table.

Every key, newest first, with its owner's email and name. Never returns the secret.

Each row carries a derived `type` — `"public"` or `"server"`. There is no type column; it's read from the key's prefix (`ak_pub_` / `ak_ser_`, with legacy `ak_live_` reported as public). Handy for auditing which users still hold legacy keys, or spotting a server key issued by mistake.

A key is a pointer to a user, plus a type. Identify the user by **either** field:

```json
{ "email": "client@acme.com" }
```
or
```json
{ "userId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" }
```

Email is an exact match against the user's stored email. Unknown user → 404 `USER_NOT_FOUND`; neither field → 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`.

## type

Optional, `"public"` (default) or `"server"`. Omitting it always gives you a public key — a forgotten field can never hand out a key that skips the origin check. An unknown value → 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`.

- `"public"` → **`ak_pub_…`**. Origin-secured: only works from a browser whose `Origin` matches the user's `allowedOrigins` (set via Update user). Wrong or missing origin → 403 `ACCESS_DENIED` with a deliberately vague "Access denied." (the real cause is visible in PostHog). This is the key you embed in a client website.
- `"server"` → **`ak_ser_…`**. No origin check: works from any origin, or from a server-side caller sending no `Origin` at all. Never ship one to a browser — it is usable from anywhere by anyone who reads it.

Both types are rate-limited to 60 requests/min per key (429 `RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`), and admin users' keys skip the origin check regardless of type.

Creating a **public** key before the user has `allowedOrigins` configured is fine — it's just dead until an admin sets them. A **server** key works immediately.

A key's type is fixed at creation (it's encoded in the prefix, there's no type column). To change it, create a new key and revoke the old one.

The response echoes the derived `type`. The full key is in the response too (also recoverable via Reveal key or Lookup user by email).

Decrypts and returns the key's full value: `{ "key": "ak_live_…" }`.

Revoked keys are never revealed — returns **410** `API_KEY_REVOKED` ("This key was revoked."). Create a new key for the user instead.

Soft revoke — the key stops authenticating but the row stays. Returns 204, or 404 `API_KEY_NOT_FOUND`. The holder starts getting 401 `API_KEY_REVOKED` immediately.

This is also **step 2 of the `ak_live_` → `ak_pub_` migration**. After running Migrate legacy keys and updating a client site to its new key, revoke that site's legacy key here. Do it one site at a time, and check the legacy key's `lastUsedAt` in List keys first — if it hasn't moved since you updated the site, nothing is still calling with it. Revoking before the site is updated takes the site down.
Hard-deletes the row (and its email logs, cascade).

query.description: Preview only — lists what would be migrated, mints nothing, and returns newKey: null. Remove or disable to actually mint.

request.description:
**Step 1 of 2** in retiring the legacy `ak_live_` prefix. Mints a fresh `ak_pub_` key for every user still on a legacy key, and returns the new key values so you can update each client site.

Safe to run: this is **purely additive**. The legacy keys are deliberately left ACTIVE, because their value is still embedded in client websites that haven't been updated. Nothing breaks when you run this — each affected user simply holds two working keys for a while.

```json
{
  "dryRun": false,
  "migrated": [
    { "userId": "…", "email": "client@acme.com", "legacyKeyId": "…", "legacyPrefix": "ak_live_a1b2c3", "newKeyId": "…", "newKey": "ak_pub_…" }
  ],
  "skipped": [],
  "next": "Update each client site to its new key, then revoke the legacy key…"
}
```

`newKey` is the full value — copy it out now; later it's recoverable via Reveal key or Lookup user by email.

## Then what

**Step 2 is manual and is the part that can break things.** For each entry: update that client's site to the new key → confirm the site works → only then revoke the legacy key with Revoke key (`DELETE /v1/admin/keys/:legacyKeyId`), using `legacyKeyId` from the response. Revoking before the site is updated takes the site down.

Check `lastUsedAt` on the legacy key in List keys before revoking — if it hasn't moved since you updated the site, nothing is calling with it anymore.

## Notes

- **Idempotent** — a user who already holds an active `ak_pub_` key is reported under `skipped` rather than getting another key, so re-running is safe.
- A user holding two legacy keys gets **one** new key, not two.
- `?dryRun=1` (as configured here) writes nothing and returns `newKey: null`. Run it first to see the scope, then disable the param to mint for real.
- Revoked legacy keys are ignored entirely.

query.description: Required. The portfolio user id whose email history to read.
Optional. Recent rows to return (default 10, max 50).

request.description:
Per-user email usage for the admin dashboard: aggregate stats plus the most recent sends.

Returns `{ stats: { total, thisMonth, send, contact, lastSentAt }, emails: [...] }`. `send` counts transactional sends via POST /v1/emails/send; `contact` counts contact-form deliveries. An unknown `userId` returns empty stats, not a 404.

This is the admin-side counterpart of GET /v1/emails, which only ever shows the calling key's own history.

item.name: Envs
item.description:
Off-machine backups of client projects' `.env` files.

**Admin-only, with no client-facing equivalent.** There is deliberately no `/v1/me/envs`: a client key lives inside someone else's codebase, so any route that hands a decrypted `.env` to a non-admin key would turn one leaked key into every credential that client owns.

**Reading one back needs two factors:** an admin key *and* the vault password, posted in the body of **Reveal env file**. Everything else here (list, create, update, delete) needs only the admin key — the password guards decryption specifically.

The content is encrypted with AES-256-GCM under `KEY_ENC_SECRET` before it is stored, so a database dump on its own leaks nothing.

Uploads take two things: the raw `.env` text and an optional `description`. Everything else (`varCount`, timestamps, the encryption) is derived server-side; sending a derived field is a 400. Env request bodies are also excluded from error telemetry, so neither a failed upload nor a failed password attempt ships anything sensitive to PostHog.

Snapshots stack up — a new upload never overwrites an older one, so a bad paste can't destroy a good backup. Deleting a user cascades their env files away with them.

request.description:
Every env snapshot, newest first, with its owner's email and name. Metadata only — `contentEnc` is never returned.

Optional filters (either one, not both): `?userId=<uuid>` or `?email=client@acme.com` (exact match). Omit both to list every client's snapshots.

`varCount` is the number of `KEY=value` lines counted at upload — a cheap way to spot a truncated or empty paste without decrypting anything.

Back up one `.env` file. Identify the owner by **either** field:

```json
{ "email": "client@acme.com" }
```
or
```json
{ "userId": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000" }
```

Unknown user → 404 `USER_NOT_FOUND`; neither field → 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`.

## content

Required. The raw `.env` text, pasted verbatim — comments, blank lines, ordering and multi-line values are all preserved byte-for-byte and come back exactly as sent. It is **not** parsed into key/value pairs. Remember to escape newlines as `\n` in the JSON body.

## description

Optional free text, max 500 chars, e.g. `"acme-site production"`. This is the only label a snapshot has — it's what you'll scan the list by later, so make it say which project and which environment.

The body is strict: any other field (`varCount`, `contentEnc`, …) → 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`. Those are derived here, never taken from the caller.

Returns **201** with the metadata row. The content is deliberately not echoed back — read it via **Reveal env file**.

body.raw:
NEXT_PUBLIC_CLERK_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=pk_test_xxx
CLERK_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_xxx

# `npx convex dev` writes these to .env.local
NEXT_PUBLIC_CONVEX_URL=https://precious-lark-922.convex.cloud

# Public by design — the agency API enforces an origin allowlist.
NEXT_PUBLIC_AGENCY_API_KEY=ak_pub_xxx
CONVEX_DEPLOYMENT=dev:precious-lark-922

request.description:
Same as **Create env file**, but you paste the `.env` in raw — no JSON, no escaping newlines.

Send `Content-Type: text/plain` (anything that isn't `application/json` works) and put the file itself in the body. The owner and label move to the query string:

- `?email=client@acme.com` or `?userId=<uuid>` — required, same rules as the JSON form.
- `?description=acme-site production` — optional.

The body is stored **exactly** as pasted: blank lines, `#` comments, ordering and spacing all survive, and **Reveal env file** hands it back byte-for-byte, ready to drop straight into a project. Nothing is parsed — `varCount` just counts `KEY=value` lines for the listing.

Empty or whitespace-only body → 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`. No user in the query → 400 with a reminder that these come from the query string here.

`PATCH /v1/admin/envs/:id` accepts the same raw form (body = new content, `?description=` optional).
One snapshot's metadata, with its owner's email and name. No content — use **Reveal env file** for that. Unknown id → 404 `ENV_FILE_NOT_FOUND`.

Decrypts the stored `.env` and serves it as `text/plain` — the file itself, byte-for-byte as it was uploaded: real newlines, blank lines and `#` comments intact. Send, then copy the response body straight into your project's `.env`.

## Two factors, both required

An admin key gets you to this endpoint. The **vault password** in the body gets you the plaintext. A leaked admin key alone cannot decrypt anything.

```json
{ "password": "…" }
```

Fill the password in yourself each time — the saved request deliberately keeps it empty so it is never stored in the collection or synced to Postman's cloud.

- Wrong password → 403 `ENV_PASSWORD_INVALID`. Checked *before* the row is looked up, so a wrong password can't be used to probe which ids exist (an unknown id also returns 403, not 404).
- 5 wrong attempts in 15 minutes → 429 `TOO_MANY_PASSWORD_ATTEMPTS` for that key.
- Missing `password` → 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`.
- Every failed attempt is reported to PostHog with the admin's email — the password itself never is.

## Why POST

A password in a query string is recorded in Worker logs, Postman history and PostHog's `request.query`. Request bodies are not, and env-route bodies are additionally excluded from telemetry buffering. There is deliberately **no GET version** of this route — it would be a passwordless path to the same plaintext.

Responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store, private`. Errors are the standard JSON envelope; only the 200 body is raw. Unknown id (with a correct password) → 404 `ENV_FILE_NOT_FOUND`.

Edits one snapshot in place. Two writable fields, both optional (send at least one, or 400 `VALIDATION_FAILED`):

- `content` — replaces the stored text; it is re-encrypted and `varCount` is recounted.
- `description` — `null` clears it.

`updatedAt` is stamped on every call. Any other field → 400.

Note this **overwrites** the old content, unlike Create which adds a new snapshot. When in doubt, create a new one instead — snapshots are cheap and the old value stays recoverable.

Unknown id → 404 `ENV_FILE_NOT_FOUND`.

Hard delete — the row is gone and the content is unrecoverable. There is no soft-delete here: a stale env snapshot has no audit value worth keeping. Returns **204**; unknown id → 404 `ENV_FILE_NOT_FOUND`.

Full breakdown of AWS SES state. Aggregates several SES Query API reads into one response:

- `account` — sending enabled, production vs sandbox (`productionAccess: false` = SES sandbox), 24h quota (`max24HourSend`), send rate (`maxSendRate`, emails/sec), `sentLast24Hours`.
- `identities` — every verified email/domain identity with `verificationStatus`; domains also carry `dkimEnabled` + `dkimStatus`.
- `statistics` — last 14 send data points (newest first): `deliveryAttempts`, `bounces`, `complaints`, `rejects` per timestamp.

Admin key required (403 ADMIN_REQUIRED otherwise). Errors: 500 EMAIL_NOT_CONFIGURED (missing AWS creds), 502 EMAIL_PROVIDER_ERROR (SES rejected a call — message is SES's own error).

request.description:
Runs all dependency probes live and returns per-check status + latency: db (Neon select 1), kv (put/get roundtrip), ses (GetAccountSendingEnabled), r2 (ListBuckets). 200 when all pass, 503 when any fail (failing check carries an error message).

Each call hits every dependency — that's why it's admin-only; the public GET /health serves the cached cron result instead.

item.description: Requires a key whose user has type "admin".
